passage.title: How a Correlation Became a Medical Myth

paragraphs.text: During the second half of the twentieth century, nutrition research came to rely heavily on a new kind of evidence. Instead of studying a few patients closely, researchers followed thousands of people for years, asked them what they ate, and recorded who later became ill. Such studies repeatedly produced striking associations. To keep the logic clear, this passage follows a simplified, generic version of a story that has occurred with more than one food, rather than any single study. In it, people who regularly ate a particular food, which we can call food X, developed heart disease less often than people who rarely ate it.

The most direct explanation is that food X itself lowers the risk. It might contain a substance that affects blood pressure or the condition of blood vessels. If this causal hypothesis is correct, it makes several predictions. People who eat more of the food should, on average, show lower risk than those who eat a little. The association should survive when researchers take other differences between eaters and non-eaters into account. Most importantly, assigning people to eat the food should reduce their chance of developing the disease.

A competing hypothesis holds that the food is a marker rather than a cause. People who choose food X may differ from others in many ways at once: they may have higher incomes, smoke less, exercise more, and see doctors more regularly. Each of these could lower disease risk on its own. This hypothesis predicts that the association will weaken as more background factors are measured, that people who eat food X will also look healthier in ways the food could not plausibly affect, and that assigning the food will make little difference.

The two hypotheses therefore split at identifiable points. One concerns adjustment: does the association shrink once income, smoking, and exercise are considered? Another concerns outcomes unrelated to any proposed mechanism. If regular eaters of food X also suffer fewer accidental injuries, the food is unlikely to be responsible, and a difference in the kind of people who eat it becomes the more probable explanation. A third point is experimental. Only a trial in which chance, rather than personal choice, decides who eats the food can break the link between the habit and the background that accompanies it.

In the generic story, the first of these checks complicated matters. When researchers examined the background of regular eaters more closely, they found that this group did tend to be wealthier, to smoke less, and to exercise more. Adjusting for those differences reduced the association but did not remove it. The remaining association was difficult to interpret. It could represent a genuine effect of the food, but it could also reflect background differences that were measured imperfectly, since questionnaires record income or exercise only roughly, or that were never measured at all.

Randomized trials and long-term follow-up studies answer different parts of the question. A trial, by assigning the food by chance, tends to balance background factors between groups, including ones nobody thought to measure. In the generic story, such a trial found little difference in disease between those assigned the food and those who were not. Trials have their own limits, however. They often last only a few years, participants do not always follow instructions, and the amount eaten may differ from everyday habits. Follow-up studies capture long periods and real behavior, but they remain exposed to the confounding the trial was designed to avoid.

Supporters of each hypothesis can therefore point to an apparent weakness in the other side's evidence. Additional observations could narrow the disagreement. A longer trial in which participants actually ate the assigned amount would test whether benefits appear only over many years. Studies in a population where food X is cheap and eaten by people of every income level would also help. If the association disappeared there, the confounding hypothesis would gain support; if it remained, the causal hypothesis would become more credible.

Returning to the opening puzzle, the story shows how a correlation can become a medical myth. The association was real and repeatedly observed, a plausible mechanism was available, and the language of research findings shifted easily from saying that the food was linked to lower risk to saying that it protected against disease. The evidence supports the first statement much more strongly than the second. The trial weakens the causal claim, although it cannot show that the food has no effect at all, since a small benefit might escape detection. The myth lay not in the correlation itself but in the leap from correlation to cause.

passage.title: The Plastic Designed to Disappear

paragraphs.text: Over the twentieth century, food packaging moved from glass, tin, and paper toward plastics that were light, cheap, and durable. Durability, once a selling point, gradually became a complaint, as discarded wrappers persisted in landfills, rivers, and coastlines. Consider a fictional firm, here called Larkfield Materials, that set out to reverse this history. Its engineers developed a film for snack bags that, under the right conditions, breaks down into water, carbon dioxide, and biomass. The bags were printed with a single word: compostable. What happened next in this invented case raises the question of what, exactly, such a label can promise.

Three components shape the answer, and the first is the polymer itself. Larkfield's film was made from long molecular chains joined by bonds that water can split, a reaction that is slow at ordinary temperatures but speeds up considerably when heat is applied. Once the chains are shortened enough, microorganisms can consume the fragments. The design was therefore not a material that vanishes on contact with nature, but one that becomes digestible only after a preliminary stage of chemical breakdown. That first stage set the pace for everything that followed.

The second component is the environment in which the film ends up, and it interacts closely with the first. An industrial composting facility maintains large heaps at high temperatures for weeks, keeps them moist, and turns them so that oxygen reaches the microbes. Under those conditions, the bonds break quickly and the fragments are consumed. In a cool garden heap, in soil, or in seawater, the same chemistry proceeds far more slowly, because the stage that depends on heat barely begins. The film's compostability was real, but it was a property of the material paired with a specific setting.

A third component is the system that carries used packaging to one setting rather than another. For the film to reach an industrial composter, a household must place it in a food-waste bin, a local authority must collect that waste, and a facility willing to accept packaging must exist within reach. Each link has its own limits. Some facilities reject packaging because it is hard to distinguish from conventional plastic, and many areas have no food-waste collection at all. Where any link is missing, the material's designed behavior never has a chance to occur.

Combine the three components and the outcomes Larkfield's early customers reported become predictable. Bags placed in home compost bins were still recognizable months later. Bags placed in recycling bins were treated as contamination, since the film could not be processed along with conventional plastics. Bags dropped as litter behaved much like the ordinary plastic they were meant to replace, at least over the period anyone was watching. None of these results showed that the chemistry had failed. They showed that it had been tested in one setting and used in others.

Larkfield's response took two directions, each addressing a different link. On the material side, its chemists explored formulations whose first stage of breakdown could begin at lower temperatures, hoping to widen the range of settings in which the film would work. On the system side, the company sought agreements with municipalities that collect food waste, added clearer disposal instructions, and made its film easier for facilities to identify. The two strategies are not alternatives. A material that degrades more easily still needs a route away from rivers and coastlines, and a better route matters only if the material behaves well at its destination.

Varying one component at a time reveals how tightly they are coupled. Suppose the collection system works perfectly but the film is unchanged: it composts well, yet only where industrial facilities exist. Suppose instead that the formulation improves but collection does not: more bags might eventually break down in garden heaps, but litter in cold water would still persist for a long time. Making the film degrade too readily raises another difficulty, since packaging must remain intact while it protects food on a shelf. Improving one component shifts where the bottleneck lies rather than removing it.

Some conclusions are secure. The film's degradation depends on conditions, its label described the material's behavior in one setting, and whether it actually disappears depends on infrastructure as much as on chemistry. Other questions remain open in this fictional case, as they do in real ones: whether lower-temperature formulations can be made without weakening the film during use, how quickly breakdown would proceed in the open environment, and whether collection systems will expand widely enough. What the case does establish is that a material property is best understood as a relationship between a substance and the social systems that handle it.

passage.title: The Language of an Underground City

paragraphs.text: Many of the underground passages beneath large cities were never planned as networks. They began as short links between a railway station and a department store, or as tunnels that let shoppers cross a busy road without waiting at traffic lights. Over the decades, new stations, office towers, and shopping corridors were attached to these links, often by different owners at different times. What had once been a few corridors became a maze with dozens of exits. The signs along these routes were added in the same piecemeal way, with each owner labeling its own section in its own style.

A common view among designers holds that the resulting confusion can be solved by a unified sign system. If every corridor used the same symbols, colors, and exit numbers, and if consistent maps were posted at each junction, people would find their way as easily below ground as above it. Analyses of existing signs seem to support this claim. In many networks, the same exit is described differently on different signs, maps face in inconsistent directions, and an arrow pointing straight ahead may mean either continue forward or climb the stairs.

The argument draws further strength from what underground spaces lack. Above ground, walkers can see the sky, distant towers, and the position of the sun, all of which help them keep track of direction. Below ground these cues disappear, and corridors that bend gradually can leave a person facing a different way without noticing. Official signs are among the few sources of information that remain. On this reasoning, improving them should help navigation more underground than anywhere else, because there is so little else to rely on.

The strongest objection comes from watching how people actually move through these spaces. Regular users rarely consult the posted maps. Instead they navigate by landmarks: a particular bakery, a fountain, the smell of a coffee stand, the place where the floor changes from tile to stone. Asked for directions, they describe sequences of such features rather than exit numbers. If people rely on landmarks instead of official representations, the objection argues, perfecting the signs will achieve little, because the signs are not what most people are reading.

This objection holds only under certain conditions. It describes regular users, whose knowledge has been built through repetition, and it may not describe visitors who have never seen the bakery or the fountain. It also assumes that landmarks are stable. Shops in underground malls change tenants frequently, and a route remembered as turning left at the flower stand fails once the stand becomes a phone shop. The objection shows that people prefer landmarks when they have them. It does not show that signs are useless to those who do not.

Consider a hypothetical redesign experiment. Suppose one underground network replaced its mixed signs with a single consistent system, while a second, similar network left its signs unchanged but added large, distinctive landmarks, such as brightly colored walls and sculptures, at its main junctions. In such a study, first-time visitors in the first network might find their exits faster, while regular users in the second might report greater confidence. If these results occurred, they would support neither side completely. Each intervention would help a different group, suggesting that the original claim and the objection describe different users rather than contradicting each other.

Both positions, however, tend to overlook people for whom neither signs nor visual landmarks work well. A person with limited vision may depend on textured paving, sound, or changes in air flow near an exit. A person who cannot read the local language may recognize pictograms but not the names of stations. For these users, the contrast between official and personal maps matters less than whether information is available through more than one sense or system. Their experience suggests that the debate has been framed too narrowly around sight.

What can be concluded is therefore conditional. It is fairly clear that the maps people carry in their heads differ from the maps that authorities post on walls, and that regular users rely on the former. It is also clear that standardized signs matter most to those who lack personal knowledge of a space. Less certain is whether a sign system could be designed to work with landmarks rather than merely alongside them, for example by naming junctions after features that people already notice. That possibility remains untested, and the hypothetical experiment can only indicate where such a test might begin.

passage.title: Why Two People Perceive the Same Sound Differently

paragraphs.text: If two people sit side by side and listen to the same recording through identical headphones, do they hear the same thing? The question can be tested, and the answer is often no. A short audio clip that circulated widely online in 2018 made the point vividly: some listeners heard the word "Laurel," others heard "Yanny," and some could not hear the alternative even after being told about it. The pressure waves reaching each listener were the same. Whatever produced the difference had to lie somewhere between the ear and the experience of hearing.

For much of the history of hearing research, the natural place to look would have been the ear itself. The prevailing picture treated hearing largely as transmission. Sound entered the ear, was broken into frequencies in the inner ear, and was passed along to the brain, which registered what had arrived. Differences between listeners were explained mainly by differences in their ears, such as hearing loss with age. This view was not foolish. It accounted for a great deal, including why the same sounds become harder to hear as the inner ear loses sensitivity.

Practical problems pushed researchers to look further. Communication systems in the mid-twentieth century required operators to follow one voice among many, and engineers wanted to know how much a listener could take in at once. Experiments that played different messages into each ear produced a striking result. Listeners asked to repeat the message in one ear could report little about the other, sometimes failing to notice that it had switched to a different language. The sound had reached both ears equally, yet only one message was heard in any detail.

The first interpretation kept as much of the older picture as possible. Attention was described as a filter placed early in processing, letting one channel through and blocking the rest. This account explained the repetition experiments well, and for a time it seemed that perception could still be treated as reception, with a gate added. But further findings did not fit neatly. Listeners sometimes noticed their own name in the ignored ear, which suggested that the unattended message had been analyzed for meaning before being set aside. The filter could not be as simple as first proposed.

A larger shift came from evidence that the brain does not simply wait for sound. When a short segment of a spoken word is replaced by a cough or a burst of noise, listeners often report hearing the missing sound and may be unable to say where the gap was. Which sound they restore can depend on words that come afterward, meaning that the experience of an earlier moment is shaped by information arriving later. Perception here appears to combine incoming signals with expectations about what is likely, filling in what the signal leaves out.

Different experimental methods reveal different parts of this process, and they are not interchangeable. Repetition studies manipulate what a listener is trying to attend to and measure what the listener can report. Restoration studies keep the listener's task constant and alter the signal, showing how expectations fill gaps. Recordings of brain activity add a third angle: when a repeated tone is occasionally replaced by a different one, the brain produces a distinctive response even if the listener is reading and ignoring the sounds. That response suggests the brain tracks regularities and registers violations without deliberate attention. Each method isolates one influence while holding others steady, so none alone tells the full story.

One consequence of this research was unexpected. If expectations shape what is heard, they can also be changed, and the same sound can be heard differently by the same person on different occasions. In sine-wave speech, a sentence is reduced to a few whistling tones, and listeners typically hear it at first as meaningless noise. Once they are told that the sounds are speech, or hear the original sentence, many can no longer avoid hearing the words. The difference between two listeners, it turned out, could be reproduced within one listener simply by changing what that person knew.

Compared with the older picture, the present one moves the source of difference from the ear alone to a combination of ear, attention, and expectation. The observations behind this change are fairly direct: identical signals produce different reports, and those reports shift with instructions and prior knowledge. The interpretation that the brain actively predicts and selects, rather than merely receiving, is more theoretical, and researchers still disagree about how prediction is carried out. Yet the evidence makes one point hard to dismiss. Hearing is not a recording of what arrives; it is partly an answer the brain constructs to the question of what is probably there.

passage.title: The Politics of Closing a Coal Plant

paragraphs.text: Why would a town's unemployment rate fall after its largest employer closed? In the fictional town of Brackwell, that is what local records showed three years after its coal-fired power plant shut down. The plant had employed several hundred people directly and supported many more jobs indirectly. Most residents expected joblessness to rise sharply. Instead, the official rate dipped slightly below its level before the closure. Read alone, the figure suggests that fears about the closure were exaggerated. Tracing how it came about, starting from the figure and working backward, produces a less comfortable picture.

First, consider what an unemployment rate counts. It includes people who are looking for work but cannot find it; it excludes those who have stopped looking, retired early, or moved away. In Brackwell, a number of former plant workers in their fifties accepted early retirement packages, and several younger families left for cities with more openings. Each departure removed someone from the calculation without creating a job. The lower rate was therefore accurate as a measurement but misleading as a sign of recovery. It described who remained in the labor market, not how the community as a whole fared.

Why did so many people leave the labor market rather than find new work? The most direct clue lies in the two policies the regional government offered. One was a retraining program paying for courses in fields such as electrical installation and health care. The other was a transfer of funds to the town council to replace the property tax the plant had paid. Retraining reached fewer workers than planned: courses lasted up to two years, the nearest training center was an hour away, and few local employers were hiring in the new fields. The transfer kept schools and other public services running, but it created no jobs on its own.

The weaknesses of retraining point to an earlier factor: the shape of the local economy before the closure. The plant had paid wages well above what most other local jobs offered, and many households had organized their mortgages and expectations around those wages. For a worker in his fifties, a two-year course leading to a lower-paid job, possibly in another town, was a poor bargain compared with an early pension. The choices that lowered the unemployment rate were, in this sense, reasonable responses to the options available, not signs of unwillingness to work.

The same factor helps explain why the closure was framed as a contest between emissions and jobs. The regional authorities had committed to cutting carbon emissions, and the plant was among the largest sources in the area. Because so much local income depended on a single facility, any plan to reduce its emissions appeared to threaten the town directly. Public debate treated one side as caring about the climate and the other about livelihoods, though many residents cared about both. The concentration of income in one employer turned a technical question about energy supply into a question about the town's future.

Going back one more step leads to the closure decision itself. The plant's operator announced the shutdown with about eighteen months' notice, after rising costs and the regional emission targets made continued operation unprofitable. The regional government designed its two policies only after this announcement. Eighteen months was long enough to fund courses but too short to attract new employers, build training facilities closer to the town, or let workers prepare gradually. In this account, the timing of the decision, more than the decision itself, limited what either policy could achieve.

Could the same result have arisen through a different route? Imagine another hypothetical town where a similar plant closes but the local economy is more varied and a training center already operates nearby. Retraining there would probably reach more workers, and fewer people would need to leave or retire early. The unemployment rate might rise for a time and then fall, but for a different reason: because people found new work. The same figure could thus reflect either recovery or withdrawal from the labor market, and it cannot by itself show which has occurred.

Put in forward order, the Brackwell sequence runs from a concentrated economy, through a closure announced on short notice and policies designed after the fact, to choices that shrank the labor force and, finally, a reassuring statistic. The sequence points to some conditions under which a transition away from coal might be considered fair: adequate lead time, support matched to workers' ages and wages, and attention to whether people can remain in the community. It does not show that retraining generally fails or that fiscal transfers suffice. It shows only that, in this case, an encouraging number concealed how the costs of reducing emissions were distributed.

passage.title: A Public Debate Over an Uncertain Model

paragraphs.text: Why would residents reject a flood forecast that, by the engineers' own testing, was more accurate than the one it replaced? The question arose in Corran Bridge, an imaginary river town used here as an illustration. Its council adopted a new computer model that redrew the map of streets likely to flood in a severe storm. On paper the change was an improvement: run against records of past floods, the new model matched the observed water levels more closely than the old map had. Yet at the first public meeting, residents greeted the map with suspicion and, in several neighborhoods, open anger.

The anger was not evenly spread. Households whose streets were newly shaded as high-risk faced higher insurance costs and building restrictions, so they had obvious reasons to object. But residents of unchanged streets complained too, and their questions were similar. Why had the lines moved? What did the shading mean: a certain flood, a likely one, or merely a possible one? Officials responded by repeating that the model had passed its tests. That reply addressed a question the residents had not quite asked, and it did little to calm the meeting.

In this scene, the chain of cause and effect seems fairly clear. The model produced a sharp-edged map, and sharp edges suggested a precision the calculations did not have. The engineers knew that the boundaries depended on assumptions about rainfall, blocked drains, and the height of river banks, each with a range of plausible values. None of that range appeared on the map. Residents, seeing a line drawn between their house and a neighbor's, reasonably read it as a firm judgment, and when they learned it could have been drawn elsewhere, they concluded that something had been concealed.

The same mechanism behaves differently under other conditions. Suppose an equally uncertain model had confirmed the boundaries people already expected. Few would have asked how it was built, and its hidden assumptions would have passed unnoticed. Or suppose the model had been plainly inaccurate, failing to match past floods; then distrust would have been a sound response to weak performance rather than to poor explanation. The reaction in Corran Bridge therefore appears to depend on a particular combination: a model good enough to be adopted, results that surprised people, and a presentation that hid the assumptions behind those results.

It would be too simple, however, to conclude that accuracy did not matter. Residents' questions eventually turned to performance as well: had the model been tested on floods like the ones their own streets had experienced? Explanation and accuracy were tangled together, because without knowing the assumptions, residents had no way to judge whether the claimed accuracy applied to them. A model may perform well on average and poorly in particular neighborhoods, and only a description of what it assumes allows people to ask where that might happen.

The council eventually tried a different approach. Engineers held smaller sessions in which they showed how the map changed when rainfall, drain blockage, or bank height was varied within the plausible range. Residents contributed information the engineers lacked, such as which drains routinely clogged with leaves each autumn. Some boundaries shifted as a result, and some objections faded, though not all; owners on newly shaded streets still faced costs they disliked. The sessions did not produce agreement on every line. They did change the dispute from whether the model could be trusted into which assumptions were reasonable for which streets.

How far does this lesson travel? It seems strongest where a model's outputs carry direct consequences for identifiable people and where those people possess local knowledge relevant to its assumptions. It may matter less for forecasts whose users simply want a single number, or where no one outside the modeling team is in a position to contribute information. Nor does sharing assumptions guarantee acceptance. A well-explained result can still be unwelcome, and opposition based on real costs is not a failure of communication.

So why did the residents of Corran Bridge reject a more accurate forecast? Not mainly because it was inaccurate, but because the way it was presented turned uncertain estimates into what looked like firm verdicts, leaving residents unable to judge the claims made for it. The broader principle is that communicating uncertainty means more than attaching an error figure to a result. It involves showing which assumptions drive the result, so that the people affected can judge where the model is likely to hold and where it deserves their doubt.

passage.title: The Island Species That Outsmarted Classification

paragraphs.text: On Inaccessible Island, a small volcanic island in the South Atlantic, lives a dark, mouse-sized bird that cannot fly. Weighing less than a typical chicken egg, the Inaccessible Island rail is the smallest flightless bird alive today. Its body plan, however, is far from unique. Rails that have lost the ability to fly are found on islands in several oceans, and many of them share the same short, rounded wings, sturdy legs, and soft, loose feathers. Birds that look this much alike, living on islands with similar conditions, seem to invite the conclusion that they belong together.

For much of the history of biology, classification relied mainly on shared physical features of this kind. Two species were placed in the same group if they resembled each other in skeleton, plumage, and proportions more closely than they resembled other species. The criterion is practical: museum specimens can be measured, and their similarities can be described and compared without special equipment. Its underlying assumption is that resemblance reflects ancestry, so that species which look alike probably inherited their features from a common ancestor rather than acquiring them separately.

In many cases the assumption serves well. Among birds whose features have not been reshaped by a strong shared pressure, resemblance in fine details of the skeleton and plumage often does track relatedness, and genetic studies have repeatedly confirmed groupings that anatomists proposed long before DNA could be read. The reasoning is straightforward. When a feature is complex and offers no obvious advantage in a particular environment, it is unlikely to have arisen twice by coincidence, so finding it in two species is good evidence that they share an origin.

The opposite case is familiar from outside the world of birds. Dolphins and sharks share a streamlined shape and fins, yet no one now classifies a dolphin as a fish; its lungs, warm blood, and way of feeding its young with milk place it among the mammals. Their shared features are ones that almost any fast swimmer benefits from, so they say more about the demands of moving through water than about ancestry. In such cases the criterion fails not because it was applied carelessly but because similar ways of life produced the resemblance.

The Inaccessible Island rail long sat uneasily between these cases. After it was described in the early twentieth century, it was judged distinctive enough to be placed in a genus of its own, Atlantisia, and its origins remained unclear. It would be easy to assume that a flightless bird on so remote an island was closely related to other flightless rails. A genetic study published in 2019 by Stervander and colleagues pointed elsewhere. The rail's closest living relatives turned out to be small South American rails that can still fly, and the researchers estimated that its ancestors reached the island roughly 1.5 million years ago.

The finding implies that those ancestors crossed thousands of kilometres of ocean on their own wings and lost the ability to fly only after they arrived. On islands without mammalian predators, flight is costly to maintain and offers little protection, so selection can favor smaller wings and stronger legs. Because such conditions recur on island after island, unrelated rails have repeatedly arrived at similar bodies. The researchers accordingly proposed moving the bird into Laterallus, the genus of its South American relatives. Its features had not been misdescribed; they had been misread as signs of a separate lineage when they largely reflected a common island way of life.

None of this makes physical description useless. Measurements of wings and legs remain essential for understanding how the rail moves through the island's dense tussock grass and how vulnerable it would be if a predator were ever introduced. A grouping such as "flightless island rails" is a sensible category for questions about ecology or conservation, where a shared way of life is exactly what matters. It misleads only when it is treated as a family tree, as if birds that live alike must share a recent ancestor.

Why, then, did a bird that resembles so many other island rails turn out to have such a different history? Its resemblance was real, but it was the kind of resemblance that islands tend to produce, and so it could not settle questions of ancestry on its own. The genetic evidence did not simply overrule anatomy; it showed which anatomical features deserved trust. In cases like this one, classification works best when several lines of evidence are weighed together: genes for relationships, features unlikely to evolve twice, and geography for how a bird could have reached its island at all.

passage.title: The Rise and Limits of Rational Expectations

paragraphs.text: Inside many economic models, every household understands how the economy works and forecasts future prices accordingly, making no error that could have been foreseen. Outside those models, when people are asked in surveys what they expect prices to do over the coming year, their answers are scattered, and they often differ noticeably from the forecasts of professional economists. One picture describes forecasters who already know the structure of the economy; the other describes people who are guessing from partial experience. Both pictures have shaped economic thinking, and the gap between them has never been fully closed.

The difference between the two pictures is not simply that one assumes accurate forecasts and the other inaccurate ones. Under the rational expectations hypothesis, people may be wrong, but their errors are not systematic: no one could predict them using the information available when the forecast was made. Under adaptive expectations, by contrast, people form forecasts mainly by extrapolating from past values, adjusting gradually when their guesses turn out wrong. The key question, then, is whether forecast errors follow a pattern that people could have noticed and corrected, and how quickly they do so.

The rational expectations approach was proposed by John Muth in 1961 and became influential in macroeconomics during the 1970s. Robert Lucas, in a 1972 paper on expectations and the neutrality of money, used it to argue that a predictable expansion of the money supply would be reflected in people's expectations and would therefore leave output largely unchanged. Only surprises could have real effects, and only temporarily, because people would initially confuse a general rise in prices with a rise in the particular prices they faced. A policy that tried to exploit such confusion systematically would soon be anticipated.

The adaptive view implies a different relationship between policy and outcomes. If people learn only from what they have already observed, a policy can affect behavior for some time before expectations catch up. Later work developed this idea into models of learning, in which people resemble statisticians who revise their estimates as new data arrive. Such models do not assume that people are foolish. They assume that understanding takes time to build, so the economy at any moment reflects the beliefs people have formed so far rather than the beliefs a perfectly informed observer would hold.

Two features of real economies widen the gap between these views. Information is unevenly distributed: a firm that sets prices for a living watches costs closely, while a household may notice only the prices of the goods it buys most often. And learning is slowed by change. When the structure of the economy shifts, even careful learners rely for a while on relationships that no longer hold, and their errors can then be systematic until enough new experience accumulates. Economists such as Lars Peter Hansen have gone further, examining how decisions are made when people are unsure which model of the economy is correct.

Comparing different phases of the business cycle shows where the two views separate. During long, stable periods, the past is a fairly reliable guide to the future, so forecasts built on experience and forecasts consistent with a correct model may be difficult to tell apart. At turning points, the views come apart. A forecast extrapolated from recent growth will be slow to anticipate a downturn, whereas a fully rational forecast would include whatever signs of the downturn were already available. Forecasters, including professional ones, have often been slow to recognize turning points, which suggests that learning matters most when conditions change.

This comparison has limits of its own. Slow recognition of a recession does not by itself refute rational expectations, since the hypothesis allows large errors when the available information genuinely gives no warning. The assumption may also fit better in some settings than others, for instance where the stakes are high and specialists gather information continuously. Moreover, in a stable environment, learning models often move toward the forecasts that rational expectations would predict. The two views thus differ less in the long run of a stable economy than in the period immediately after something important has changed.

What survives from this debate is a clearer sense of what the assumption is for. Rational expectations serves as a discipline: it prevents economists from building models in which people can be fooled by the same policy again and again, and that lesson has proved durable. Its limits appear where information is unequal and the economy is changing, since those are the conditions in which learning takes time. How quickly people learn, and how much expectations differ across groups, remain open questions. The assumption remains useful as long as it is treated as a benchmark rather than as a description of how people actually form expectations.

passage.title: The Archive That Digitized Its Biases

paragraphs.text: In the reading room of the Kessel County Record Office, an invented regional archive used throughout this passage, one box holds the minutes of a nineteenth-century landowners' association, catalogued folder by folder with names, dates, and subjects. On a lower shelf, a bundle of letters written by domestic servants and seasonal laborers sits under a single line: "Miscellaneous correspondence, undated." Both collections were scanned in the same digitization project. Online, a search for almost any local family name returns dozens of pages from the minutes and almost nothing from the letters. An appealing conclusion follows: the digital archive has amplified the biases of its old catalogue. It deserves testing before it is accepted.

Several facts can be observed directly. The project scanned every item in the record office, so the letters are present online as images. Searching, however, depends on catalogue descriptions and on text that software could read automatically from typed documents. The minutes survive in later typed copies and are described in detail; the letters are handwritten and described only as a group. Usage records show that online visits have risen sharply since the project was completed, and that most of them reach items with detailed descriptions.

This evidence supports one part of the hypothesis well. Search results depend on descriptions, and descriptions were unequal before any scanning began. When researchers once came in person, an archivist might mention the uncatalogued letters, or a curious visitor might open the box simply because it sat nearby. A search engine offers no such detour. It returns what it can match, ranks the matches, and displays them on a screen that most users never scroll beyond. The unevenness of the old catalogue is therefore not merely carried over; its consequences are concentrated.

What the evidence cannot show is that the difference in use reflects a difference in what researchers would have chosen had access been equal. The records show which items were opened, not which items people looked for and failed to find. Some users may simply have been more interested in landowners' affairs. Nor do the records show that the earlier, in-person system was fairer in practice. Visits were few, required travel, and depended on an archivist's attention, which may itself have favored familiar collections.

Other factors complicate the picture further. Handwritten letters are slower to read than typed minutes, so even researchers who find them may cite them less often. The letters also contain few surnames, because their writers usually referred to employers by title and signed with first names alone, so name searches would miss them under any catalogue. And the invented case includes at least one counterexample: a local historian who browsed the scanned images page by page located several letters and built a study around them. Amplification occurred, but it was not the only mechanism at work.

The record office's response offers additional, partial evidence. Staff rewrote the descriptions of the correspondence, listing writers, places, and recurring topics, and added subject headings such as "domestic service" that had never appeared in the catalogue. They also began collecting papers from families whose histories were thinly represented. Afterward, searches on those subjects began returning the letters, and visits to them increased, though only modestly, while the minutes remained the most visited items. This suggests that description, not merely the documents' presence online, governed what could be seen. It does not show that the new visitors came from the communities whose lives the letters record.

A rival explanation therefore survives under specific conditions. If users' interests were already narrow and changed little after the redescription, much of the original imbalance would reflect demand rather than the catalogue. The modest size of the increase is consistent with that possibility, as is the fact that the detailed minutes remained the most visited items. Separating the two explanations would require information the records do not contain, such as what users were searching for and why they stopped.

The case thus supports a narrower claim than the one that opened the inquiry. It is observed that digitization multiplied access and that the gains flowed mostly to well-described items. It is an interpretation, though a reasonable one, that the catalogue's inherited emphasis produced much of this pattern. What follows with some confidence is that wider access alone does not make an archive fair, because what can be found depends on choices about description and collection made long before anyone switched on a scanner.

passage.title: Can Drought Insurance Help Small Farmers?

paragraphs.text: On the wall of a small district office, in the hypothetical farming region used throughout this passage, hangs a chart of rainfall recorded at the town's weather station. For one season the line rises steadily, crossing the level that the local drought insurance contract treats as adequate. A farmer whose maize field lies on a slope some fifteen kilometers from the station looks at the same chart with frustration. Her rain came late and stopped early, and much of her crop withered before the grain could form. Her policy paid nothing, because by the measure written into the contract, there had been no drought.

The contract she bought is a form of weather index insurance. Conventional crop insurance pays according to losses on each farm, which requires inspectors to visit fields, estimate damage, and settle disputes. For holdings of a hectare or two, the cost of such visits can exceed what the policy is worth. An index contract avoids that expense by paying whenever a measured quantity, such as seasonal rainfall at a station, falls below an agreed trigger. Because no farmer can influence the rain gauge, there is little room for exaggerated claims, and payments can be made quickly once the figures are published.

The idea behind the product is simple, but it changes what is being insured. A farmer does not actually receive protection against her own losses; she receives a payment linked to a number that is expected to move together with those losses. Economists call the gap between the two basis risk. It can work in either direction. A farmer may suffer heavy losses while the index stays above the trigger, as happened on the slope, or a payment may arrive in a year when her own harvest was reasonably good.

A second scene, in the same imagined region, looks very different. Another farmer cultivates land a short walk from the station, on soil much like the ground beneath it. In a year when the rains largely failed, both the gauge and her field registered the shortfall. The payment arrived within weeks, before the next planting season, and she used it to buy seed instead of selling the goats she kept as savings. For her, the index behaved almost exactly like a measure of her own losses, and the contract did what its designers hoped.

Set side by side, the two scenes involve the same contract and the same station. What separates them is how closely the index tracks each farm. Distance matters, because rainfall can vary sharply across short stretches of land. So does timing: a seasonal total can look adequate even when a dry spell coincides with the weeks in which a crop is flowering. Soil and slope also determine how much water a field retains. Basis risk, in other words, is not simply bad luck spread evenly among farmers. Some are systematically better matched to the index than others.

Consider a fictional cooperative that offers its members two contracts. The first is cheap and pays according to total seasonal rainfall at the district station. The second costs roughly twice as much, uses rainfall during the critical growing weeks at several nearby points, and allows a field review when many members report losses that the index has missed. The second contract should produce fewer mismatches, but the review takes time, and the higher premium means that the poorest members are more likely to choose the first. Reducing basis risk, the comparison suggests, is possible, but it has a price, and that price is not borne equally.

Returning to the farmer on the slope, her case can now be read more precisely. Under the second contract, the dry weeks around flowering might have triggered a payment, or a review might have recognized her losses, though neither outcome is guaranteed for a field so far from any measuring point. What made her experience so damaging was not only the lost harvest but also the premium she had paid for protection that did not appear when she needed it. In a year like that, the policy took her money and returned none.

The two scenes and the cooperative's choice suggest a way to evaluate such products, though only within limits. The relevant question is not whether an index contract pays out on average, but how often it pays when a policyholder suffers a serious loss, and at what cost. Where the index matches farm conditions closely, a modest premium may buy meaningful protection. Where it does not, the same premium may buy a payment that arrives at the wrong time or not at all. The hypothetical cases cannot show how common either situation is in any real region.

passage.title: The Surprising Limits of Super-Resolution

paragraphs.text: On the left of the screen is a microscope image of a cell, soft and slightly blurred, in which thin filaments merge into a hazy web. On the right is the same image after processing by super-resolution software. The filaments now appear as crisp, separate lines, and small gaps between structures have become visible. Most people who see such a pair react in the same way: the software seems to have uncovered what was in the cell all along, as if a layer of fog had simply been wiped from a window.

That reaction is not unreasonable. Some restoration methods really do recover information that is present but difficult to see. If the way a microscope blurs a point of light is known, part of that blurring can be reversed mathematically, and combining many images of the same sample can reduce random noise. Restored images frequently resemble images of the same samples taken with more powerful instruments, and the structures they show often look biologically sensible. It is easy to conclude that a sharper result is simply a more truthful one.

The picture becomes less simple with methods that learn from examples. Such a method is trained on pairs of images, each consisting of a low-resolution version and a high-resolution version of the same kind of sample, and it learns to produce the second from the first. When applied to a new image, it often generates edges and textures that look finer than anything the input appears to contain. This raises a question the original intuition tends to skip: where does the additional detail come from, the measurement or the training?

The difficulty is that a blurred image is consistent with many different sharp originals. Two filaments close together and a single wide one may produce nearly the same blur. A learned method must choose among such possibilities, and it tends to choose ones that resemble what it saw during training. When a new sample matches the training material, that choice is often correct. When it differs, perhaps because the cell type or the staining has changed, the method can produce a filament that continues across a real gap or a regular texture that the sample does not have.

At least three explanations for extra detail therefore compete. The detail might be genuinely recovered information that blur and noise had hidden. It might be supplied by patterns learned during training. Or it might be an artifact of the processing itself, such as the faint ripples that can appear beside sharp edges whatever the training material. These explanations make different predictions. Recovered detail should appear consistently across repeated images of the same sample, learned detail should change when the training set changes, and edge artifacts should cluster near strong boundaries regardless of what the method was trained on.

Two kinds of test help to separate them. The first uses known samples, structures whose true geometry has been established independently, such as manufactured patterns with precisely measured spacing. Comparing the restored image with the known structure shows where the method adds, removes, or distorts features. The second is blind evaluation, in which judges compare images without knowing which were processed and which came from an independent high-resolution measurement, so that their expectations cannot guide the verdict. Neither test is complete. Known samples are often simpler than living cells, and a method that passes them may still fail on an unfamiliar specimen.

The original intuition remains appropriate in some situations. When restoration rests mainly on known physical properties of the instrument and on repeated measurements, the detail it recovers is well supported, because little is being supplied by assumptions about what samples usually look like. Learned methods can also be valuable when the task does not depend on their finest output, for instance when a researcher needs to locate large structures or follow their movement over time. In such uses, an uncertain fine texture does not change the conclusion that is drawn.

What the evidence supports is a narrower claim than the first reaction suggested. A restored image is not a direct observation; it is an estimate that combines measurement with assumptions, some explicit and some learned. Features that have been confirmed on known samples and agree with independent measurements at the same scale can reasonably be treated as observed at that scale. Finer features that have not been checked in this way are better treated as hypotheses about the sample. Where that boundary lies depends on the method, the sample, and the tests performed, and it must be established for each use rather than assumed.

passage.title: A Four-Day Week with Unequal Outcomes

paragraphs.text: On the wall of the staff kitchen at a fictional insurance company, here called Halden Mutual, a chart appeared six months after the firm moved to a four-day working week. It showed a single line for average employee satisfaction, rising steadily from the month the change began. Managers pointed to it with some pride. A visitor reading the chart, however, could fairly ask what a single line conceals. Halden employs analysts who work mostly at screens and staff who serve customers in branches and on the phone. Had the new schedule worked for the company, or only for some of the people in it?

Judged by company-wide averages, the trial looked like a success. The satisfaction survey improved, reported sick days fell, and output per hour worked rose, partly because a shorter week pushed teams to cut long meetings and routine reporting. Total output stayed roughly level despite fewer hours. Managers also noted that staff turnover in the first six months was no higher than in the previous year, which suggested the change had not driven people away. For a board deciding whether to keep the policy, these figures answered the obvious question: the firm had not lost productivity, and its employees, on average, said they were happier.

A second view of the same figures told a different story. When results were broken down by department, the gains were concentrated among analysts and other staff whose work could be compressed or rearranged. Customer-facing teams showed little improvement in satisfaction, and in some branches it declined. Their workload had not shrunk along with their week. Customers still arrived five days a week and phones still rang, so the same volume of contact had to be handled by fewer people on any given day or covered through rotating rosters that left little room for breaks.

The two pictures do not contradict each other; they arise from the same data viewed at different scales. An average combines groups of unequal size and unequal experience. Because analysts made up most of Halden's workforce, their large improvement could lift the company figure even while a smaller group was doing worse. The chart in the kitchen was accurate. What it could not show was that the improvement was distributed unevenly, and that the staff customers actually meet were carrying much of the cost.

This creates a specific trap in evaluation. It is tempting to explain the weaker results among face-to-face staff as a matter of attitude, as if they simply needed more time to adapt. The structure of their work suggests another reason. Knowledge work often contains slack that a shorter week can remove: unnecessary meetings, duplicated reports, time spent waiting for approvals. Work that consists of responding to customers in real time contains far less of that slack. Removing a day therefore improved efficiency in one kind of job and intensified pressure in the other.

Halden's managers eventually changed the scheme department by department, and those changes allow the earlier results to be read differently. Branch staff moved to staggered schedules, so that each person worked four days while the branch stayed open five, and the firm hired additional part-time staff for peak hours. After these adjustments, satisfaction among customer-facing teams began to rise, though more slowly than it had among analysts. The redesign suggests that the original problem may not have been the four-day week as such, but a single design applied to jobs with very different demands.

Each scale serves a purpose. A company average is a reasonable answer to the question of whether the policy is affordable for the firm as a whole. Department-level figures are better suited to asking who benefits and who bears the cost. Even these, however, have limits. Halden's departmental results changed after several adjustments were made at once, including new hiring, so the improvement cannot be credited to staggered schedules alone. And within each department, individuals with caring duties or long commutes might have experienced the change differently again.

Return, then, to the chart on the kitchen wall. Did the four-day week work? For the firm as a whole, by the measures it chose, it largely did. For analysts, it brought clear gains. For customer-facing staff, the original version shifted pressure onto them, and the redesigned version reduced but did not erase the gap. The answer depends on the scale of measurement, and the rising line was not wrong so much as incomplete: it reported an average effect while hiding the differences of which that effect was composed.

passage.title: When More Data Produces Less Knowledge

paragraphs.text: A century ago, measuring a factory, a river, or a city usually meant sending a person to take a reading. A technician might record the temperature of a boiler a few times a day, and a hydrologist might visit a river gauge once a week. Data were scarce because each observation cost time and labor. Inexpensive electronic sensors have changed this. A single machine can now report its temperature, vibration, and power use every second, and a city can log traffic at thousands of points at once. The change raises a question that can be examined: does a vast increase in recorded information bring a matching increase in understanding?

The question matters because more data is often assumed to be the main route to better explanations. If earlier investigators lacked answers because they lacked observations, it seems to follow that abundant observations should reveal causes that were previously hidden. This expectation is not unreasonable. Many discoveries have depended on new instruments that made previously invisible patterns measurable. The issue is whether the relationship holds generally, so that more data reliably yields more knowledge, or whether it depends on how data are collected and used.

One kind of evidence comes from cases in which large data sets have supported accurate predictions. Systems trained on records of past machine failures can often warn that a component is likely to break, and patterns in large volumes of online activity have been used to estimate trends before official statistics are published. Such successes show that abundant data can reveal dependable regularities. Their scope, however, is limited to prediction. A system can learn that a certain vibration usually precedes a failure without indicating what causes the vibration, or what would happen if operating conditions changed.

A second kind of evidence comes from what happens to such predictions when circumstances shift. A widely discussed example is Google Flu Trends, which estimated influenza activity from internet search queries. After early success, it substantially overestimated flu levels in the 2012 to 2013 season. Among the explanations later proposed were changes in how people searched and in how the search engine itself operated. Whatever the precise cause, the episode shows that a pattern found in large data can break down when the processes producing the data change, because the pattern was never tied to an understanding of those processes.

These two kinds of evidence seem to point in different directions. One suggests that more data improves our ability to anticipate events; the other suggests that this improvement can be fragile. The apparent conflict dissolves once prediction and causal explanation are distinguished. Data volume can strengthen predictions within familiar conditions without advancing explanation at all. Indeed, the more variables are recorded, the more correlations will appear by chance alone, so a researcher who searches without a guiding question may find a growing number of patterns while understanding fewer of them.

What turns data into explanation is often the design of the inquiry. A hypothesis specifies which variables should matter and what should happen if they are altered, and it directs attention toward observations that could prove it wrong. The physician John Snow's investigation of a cholera outbreak in London in 1854 is frequently cited in this context. By mapping deaths and comparing households supplied by different water sources, he examined evidence that could have contradicted his suspicion that contaminated water spread the disease. His records were small by modern standards, but they were gathered to test a claim.

This does not mean that large data sets are useless for explanation, and it would be too simple to treat hypotheses as the only source of insight. Exploratory analysis of abundant data can suggest relationships that no one thought to look for, and these can then become hypotheses to test. Some fields also exploit natural variation within large data, comparing cases that differ in a single factor, to approach causal conclusions. The real issue is not whether data or theory wins, but whether a given analysis includes some way of exposing its patterns to possible counterexamples.

The answer to the original question is therefore qualified. It is well supported that more data can improve prediction and that it does not, by itself, produce causal understanding; an abundance of variables can even multiply misleading patterns. It is also reasonably clear that hypotheses and the deliberate search for counterexamples help convert information into explanation. What remains uncertain is how far new methods for analyzing large data sets can reduce the need for prior hypotheses, a question on which the evidence is still developing.

passage.title: The Road That Followed an Ancient Tax Border

paragraphs.text: In the mid-twentieth century, a narrow lane crossing a farming plain was widened and paved to carry trucks between two market towns. Engineers left one long, gentle curve in place, because buying the land needed to cut across it would have cost more than it saved. Today drivers swing northward for several kilometers and then return, although the plain on either side looks flat. The road in this account is a composite, modeled on cases that historical geographers study in parts of Europe once under Roman rule. Why does a route bend where nothing seems to require it?

Field maps from the nineteenth century show the lane already following the same curve. On one side of it, the field boundaries form a regular pattern of long parallel lines, evenly spaced; on the other side the fields are irregular. Patterns like the regular one are often interpreted as remains of Roman land division, in which surveyors laid out a grid so that land could be allotted, recorded, and, in many provinces, taxed. If that interpretation applies here, the lane follows the outer edge of the grid, the line between land that was measured and registered and land that was not.

Consider a different history. Suppose no grid had ever been laid out on the plain. A path between the two towns would then have been shaped by other forces: the line of firm ground, the location of fords, the edges of whatever farms happened to form. On flat terrain, such a path might have run fairly directly between the towns. The long curve that drivers follow today would have had no particular reason to exist. The tax-border explanation, in other words, is a claim that the curve depends on the grid.

That claim rests on assumptions worth stating. It assumes that people traveling between the towns would otherwise have preferred a shorter route, and that something made the boundary line more attractive or more permissible than a direct one. A boundary could provide exactly this. A strip along the edge of registered land might belong to no individual holding, so walking along it trespassed on no one's fields, and over time a path wore into it. The explanation also assumes that the boundary stayed visible and respected long enough for the path to become fixed in local habit.

The difficulty is that a survey boundary is not independent of the landscape. Surveyors often ended a grid where the land became less useful: at the edge of a marsh, along a river terrace, or where slopes began. If the grid stopped at such a feature, then both the boundary and the road may have followed the feature, and the grid would be a fellow traveler rather than a cause. Later centuries add confusion: medieval estates, parish limits, and drainage works could reuse an old line or create a new one in the same place.

Comparing cadastral maps with terrain data offers a way to weigh these explanations. Where the curve coincides with a slight rise or an old watercourse, terrain alone could account for it, and the boundary explanation adds little. Where the curve crosses ground that shows no such feature, yet still matches the edge of the regular field pattern, the case for the boundary grows stronger. If the field lines on one side share the angle and spacing of a grid documented elsewhere in the region, while the road traces their outer limit, coincidence becomes harder to sustain.

Even favorable evidence stops short of proof. The history in which no grid existed cannot be observed, so the claim that the road would otherwise have run straight remains an estimate. The nineteenth-century maps record the landscape many centuries after any Roman survey, and the regular pattern could have been extended or reshaped in the meantime. Dating a line on the ground is hard, because the same ditch or path may have been dug, abandoned, and recut many times. A close match between road and grid edge shows that the two are connected; it does not reveal when or how the connection began.

The observations are that the road follows a curve with little basis in present terrain, and that the curve traces the edge of a field pattern of a type associated with Roman land division. The interpretation is that an administrative line, drawn to measure and assess land, shaped how people later moved across it, and so survived long after the system that created it had disappeared. That interpretation is plausible and, where terrain offers no rival explanation, well supported. It suggests that institutions can leave traces in space that outlast the institutions themselves.

passage.title: The Unexpected Winners of a Subsidy

paragraphs.text: For most of its history, the fictional city of Lindmoor helped low-income tenants mainly by building public housing. As construction budgets shrank and waiting lists grew, the city council turned to a different tool: a subsidy paid toward the private rents of eligible households. The program expanded in stages, and within two decades it covered tens of thousands of households. Its supporters argued that a subsidy would let families choose where to live and reach far more people than new buildings ever could. The question that later occupied researchers was simpler to state than to answer: who, in the end, received the money?

The first evaluations looked encouraging. Surveys of participating households found that most lived in units of acceptable quality and that the share of income they spent on rent had fallen. Officials explained these results in the most direct way: the subsidy reduced what tenants paid, and the savings went to food, transport, and other needs. Because each payment was made on the tenant's behalf, it seemed natural to treat tenants as the program's beneficiaries. Nothing in these early surveys contradicted that view, but nothing in them tested it either.

Doubts arose from a different kind of record. A housing advocacy group compiling online listings noticed that advertised rents for small apartments in several districts had risen faster than rents in neighboring towns without a similar program. In some buildings, subsidized tenants appeared to be charged more than unsubsidized tenants for comparable units. If landlords were raising rents in response to the subsidy, part of each payment would be passing through tenants to property owners. The observation was suggestive rather than conclusive, since rents might have been rising for reasons unrelated to the program.

Separating these explanations required more careful comparisons. Analysts commissioned by the city matched listings over time, comparing units of similar size and condition, and tracked rents before and after each stage of expansion. They also distinguished between districts. Some had many vacant apartments and active construction; others had almost no vacancies, and new building there was restricted by zoning rules and a shortage of land. The analysts also checked whether renovations could account for higher rents, since a higher price for a better unit is not the same as a higher price for the same unit.

The reasoning behind the original suspicion was straightforward once it was spelled out. A subsidy increases the amount that eligible tenants are able to pay. If the number of available apartments cannot grow quickly, more money competing for the same units tends to push their prices up. A landlord who knows that a tenant can now afford more has less reason to accept a lower rent. In that situation, some of the subsidy ends up as higher rent rather than lower housing costs, even though every payment is formally made on the tenant's behalf.

The district comparisons gave this reasoning a measurable shape. Where vacancies were plentiful and new housing could be built, rents for comparable units rose little after each expansion, and tenants appeared to keep most of the benefit. Where vacancies were scarce and building was restricted, rents for comparable units rose noticeably, and a larger share of the subsidy appeared to reach landlords. The same program, in other words, did not have a single effect. How its benefits were divided depended less on its own rules than on the condition of the housing market into which the money flowed.

Several questions remained open. The analysts could not fully rule out the possibility that tenants in tight districts were choosing better apartments in ways the data did not capture. Higher rents might also have encouraged some owners to maintain buildings they would otherwise have neglected, a benefit that is difficult to measure. Evaluating the program therefore required more than one indicator: the share of income tenants paid, the rents of comparable units, and the condition of the housing stock each captured a different part of the picture.

Looking back, Lindmoor's understanding of its subsidy changed in stages. It began with the assumption that the households named in the program were its only beneficiaries, moved through a suspicion based on rising listings, and arrived at comparisons showing that the answer differed by district. What was observed is that rents for comparable units rose more where supply was constrained. That landlords captured part of the subsidy there is an interpretation, and a well-supported one, but it rests on comparisons rather than on direct records of who gained. The gap between a program's named recipients and its actual beneficiaries turned out to be something to investigate, not assume.

passage.title: What Residue on a Jar Cannot Prove

paragraphs.text: Can the fat soaked into the wall of an ancient jar tell us what people cooked in it? The question is testable, at least in part. Unglazed pottery is porous, and when food is heated in it, some fats and oils are absorbed into the clay, where they can survive long after any visible trace has vanished. Chemists can extract these lipids from a fragment, identify their molecular components, and compare them with reference fats from known sources. Imagine, then, a single fragment of a cooking jar from an excavated house, sent to a laboratory with a simple request: identify the meal.

From the chemist's position, the task is one of identification and its limits. The extract may contain fatty acids common to many foods, together with rarer compounds that point to particular sources, such as plant waxes or substances formed when fish oils are heated. Measuring the isotopic composition of specific fatty acids can also help separate fats of ruminant animals, such as cattle and sheep, from those of pigs, and dairy fat from meat fat. Yet what the chemist reports is which molecules are present and in what proportions. The result is a chemical profile, not a recipe.

The excavating archaeologist approaches the same fragment with different aims. Where the jar was found, what lay beside it, whether its outer surface bears soot, and how its shape compares with other vessels on the site all bear on how it was used. The archaeologist wants to know about activities: cooking, storage, serving, or ritual. These questions are broader than the chemical ones, but the evidence behind them is also more indirect, since the place where an object was finally discarded may not reflect where or how it was used during its working life.

On some points the two perspectives agree without difficulty. If the fragment yields abundant animal fat with the isotopic signature of dairy products, and the jar has a form suited to heating and soot on its exterior, both specialists will accept that it probably held dairy foods at some stage, most likely over a fire. Agreement of this kind is valuable precisely because the lines of evidence are independent of each other: the chemistry does not depend on the vessel's shape, and the shape does not depend on the chemistry.

Interpretation divides when the profile is mixed or the burial conditions are uncertain. A jar used for years may have held milk, then meat stews, then stored oil, and the absorbed residue blends these episodes into something like a single average. The chemist cannot reliably say which use came first or how often each occurred. A further problem is that lipids in the surrounding soil, from decaying plants or animals, can migrate into a buried sherd. A signal that looks like food might therefore come partly from the ground in which the fragment lay.

A third perspective, that of a food historian or an anthropologist studying how communities eat, adds another layer. For this specialist, the interesting question is not only which substances entered the jar but what they meant: whether dairy foods were everyday fare or reserved for festivals, and whether cooking meat and milk in one vessel was ordinary or avoided. Chemistry cannot answer such questions directly. A residue identical in composition could come from a daily porridge or from a once-a-year offering, and the jar would preserve no difference between them.

Control samples and contextual records serve each specialist differently. For the chemist, analyzing soil collected beside the fragment, and comparing the inner and outer surfaces of the sherd, helps estimate how much of the signal came from burial rather than use. For the archaeologist, comparing many vessels of the same type from the same layer shows whether one jar's profile is typical or unusual. For the food historian, written sources, images, or later practices in the region, where they exist, offer some guidance on meaning, though they may describe a different period or social group.

What can be settled, then, depends on which claim is being made. That certain compounds are present, and that some probably derive from use rather than soil, can be established with reasonable confidence when controls are in place. That a jar was used for heating dairy products may be supported when chemistry and context agree. That the food carried a particular social or ritual significance requires evidence of a different kind, which the residue alone cannot supply. Keeping these claims separate does not reduce the value of the chemistry; it identifies the questions the chemistry is able to answer.
