passage.title: The Game That Rewarded the Wrong Strategy

paragraphs.text: How much electricity did the players of Lumen League actually save? Lumen League, an energy-saving game invented for this discussion, read each household's smart meter during a baseline week at sign-up and then awarded points for every kilowatt-hour used below that baseline, ranking players on a public leaderboard. At the end of a three-month season, the app reported an average reduction of 18 percent. The utility's bills for the same homes, compared with the same months a year earlier, showed about 6 percent. Within two months of the season's end, even that difference had disappeared.

One hypothesis treats the gap as an innocent flaw in measurement. Most baseline weeks fell during an early-winter cold spell. If many baselines happened to be unusually high, every later week would look like a saving even if behavior barely changed. On this view, players did reduce their use modestly, as the bills show, and the rest of the 18 percent belongs to the yardstick rather than to the players. The hypothesis also predicts that the gap should be spread fairly evenly across households, whatever their rank.

A second hypothesis locates the problem in what the game rewarded. Points depended not on using little electricity but on using less than one's own baseline, and a competitive player has two ways to widen that difference: lower current use or raise the baseline. The weekly rankings also favored short bursts of effort before each update rather than lasting changes in routine. If this hypothesis is right, the gap between the app and the bills should be concentrated among the most competitive players, and their savings should fade quickly once there is nothing left to win.

The two hypotheses therefore disagree about where the missing savings should be found. A measurement artifact should affect leaders and casual players alike, and households that never joined the game should show a similar apparent saving if their own meters were judged against the same cold week. Strategic play predicts a different pattern: a large gap at the top of the leaderboard, a smaller one further down, and no apparent saving among non-players. Because the utility held meter data for the whole town, this comparison could be made without relying on anything the app had recorded.

When the comparison was made, it gave neither hypothesis a clean victory. Non-players did show a small apparent saving against the cold week, as the first hypothesis predicted. The top fifty players, however, showed something more: their baseline weeks contained use far above their usual levels, and several later described on the app's forum how they had deliberately inflated their starting figures. Yet those same players had also cut their use more than average during the season. Manipulation and genuine effort were mixed within the same households, so no single share of the gap could be assigned to either cause.

The developers then tried a different design. In the second season, players joined neighborhood teams, the individual leaderboard was removed, and team points were based on utility bills compared with the same month of the previous year, a baseline no one could inflate in advance. The app now reported savings of 5 percent, close to the bills, and six months after the season ended, participating homes still used about 3 percent less than a year earlier. The first hypothesis explains the smaller reported figure, since the unreliable yardstick was gone, but says little about the persistence, which the second hypothesis attributes to a game that no longer rewarded tricks or bursts.

The contrast between the seasons is weaker evidence than it looks. The second season came later in the year, many of its players were committed people who had stayed on after the first, and two features of the design changed at once: the reward became shared, and the baseline became harder to manipulate. A sharper test would randomly assign households, during the same months, to individual or team scoring while judging both against the previous year's bills. If team players still saved more over the following year, cooperation itself, and not merely an honest yardstick, would deserve the credit.

What, then, did the first season's players save? The evidence supports a modest and short-lived real reduction, close to the bills' 6 percent, surrounded by an inflated figure produced partly by an unlucky baseline and partly by players who discovered that the scoring rule could be beaten without saving energy. That is the paradox the game exposed: the design that generated the most impressive number also gave players the strongest reason to aim at the number itself. Whether rewarding cooperation builds lasting habits remains a promising possibility rather than an established finding.

passage.title: The Puzzle of Falling Birth Rates in Prosperous Cities

paragraphs.text: If higher incomes made it easier to raise children, wealthy cities should record more births per woman than poorer regions of the same country. In many countries the pattern runs the other way: large prosperous cities frequently have fertility rates below the national average, and well below the level of about 2.1 children per woman that keeps a population stable without migration. The phenomenon has a specific shape. Surveys in many countries find that people often report wanting more children than they eventually have. The puzzle, then, is less a lack of desire than a gap between intentions and outcomes.

The first element is housing. Prosperous cities attract workers and businesses, and the resulting competition for space makes homes expensive, especially homes large enough for a family. Many couples respond by waiting until they can afford more room. Postponement might seem to change only the timing of births, not their number. Yet the ability to conceive declines with age, and plans made at thirty-five face a shorter horizon than plans made at twenty-five. A cost that first appears as a delay can therefore turn into a smaller completed family, even when the intention to have children remains unchanged.

Work practices form a second element, and they interact with the first. Jobs concentrated in prosperous cities often reward long hours and continuous availability, and the years in which careers are established tend to overlap with the years in which people have children. Couples who seek cheaper housing at the edge of a city must usually accept longer commutes. The money saved on rent or a mortgage is thus paid for in time, and time is precisely what demanding jobs have already made scarce. Neither element alone captures this exchange, which appears only when the two are considered together.

A third element concerns values and expectations about family life. Where parents feel that each child requires intensive investment, such as extended education and close supervision, the expected cost of every additional child rises. Norms about who provides care matter as well: when both partners work but care falls mainly on one of them, that partner bears most of the strain. This element has clear boundaries. Values differ across groups and change slowly, and they are harder to measure than rents or working hours. They are not simply products of the other two elements, though they are not independent of them either.

These elements explain why income alone predicts urban fertility poorly. Higher income increases the ability to pay for housing and care, but in a prosperous city it arrives together with higher prices and a higher value placed on each hour of work. Two households with the same income may face very different situations: one may have secure housing and flexible hours, while the other rents a small apartment and works long days far from home. What matters is income relative to the costs a household faces, and many of those costs are set by the city in which it lives.

Taken together, the elements operate as a mechanism rather than a list. High housing costs encourage postponement; demanding work makes the postponed years a period of career building that is hard to interrupt; intensive parenting norms raise the expected burden of each further child. Each pressure makes the others harder to escape. For this reason the combined effect resembles multiplication more than addition. A couple facing all three may decide against a second child even if any single pressure, faced alone, would have seemed manageable. The decision reflects the combination, not the largest individual cost.

Considering what happens when only one element changes makes the point clearer. Suppose a city made family housing substantially cheaper while working hours and parenting norms stayed the same. Some couples might have children earlier, but those for whom time is the binding constraint would see little difference. Flexible working arrangements without housing reform might help mainly those who are already adequately housed. Comparisons of family policies across countries are often used to estimate such effects, but they face the same difficulty: each policy enters a particular combination of housing, work, and norms, and its effect depends on that combination.

Some conclusions follow with reasonable confidence. Income by itself cannot account for low fertility in prosperous cities, and explanations that blame a single cause, whether housing, careers, or changing values, misdescribe a process in which the causes reinforce one another. Other matters remain uncertain: the relative weight of each element in a given city, how far values follow economic conditions rather than shape them, and whether births that are postponed are later recovered. The puzzle of prosperous cities is therefore best understood not as a mystery about wealth but as the outcome of several pressures acting at once.
